descriptionText:
There are numerous examples in the Etymology where a final [l], [r], [n], [m] became syllabic after another consonant and developed an intervening vowel. This vowel was [o] in most cases, but was [u] in the case of final [m]: M > Dor. (EtyAC/KHIS).

It seems this change did not occur for certain favored combinations, where which retained. There are several examples in which final [-rn] did not develop a vowel, such as Dor. or Ilk. (Ety/DORON, YAR). There is one case in which final [-lm] did not develop a vowel: Ilk. (Ety/ALAM), but another where it did: Ilk. (Ety/TAL). The two examples are very similar, so they may represent some uncertainly on Tolkiens part on the development of final [-lm] in Ilkorin.
This rule was described in the Comparative Tables (PE19/25), but there are no attested examples.

The voiceless labial stop survived initially from Primitive Elvish into Ilkorin (PE19/18), but it became [b] after vowels (PE19/23) and became [f] after liquids and voiceless stops. It was preserved medially in a few clusters, notably [sp].
The liquid sound [r] survived from Primitive Elvish into Ilkorin (PE19/19, 24).

A voiceless liquid [r] developed in Ilkorin from the initial clusters [khr] and [sr] (PE19/21). It seems likely the change would have occurred medially as well for the cluster [khr], though there it may have become a long voiceless [rr].

The voiceless sibilant sound [s] usually survived from Primitive Elvish into Ilkorin (PE19/19, 23), though primitive initial [s] vanished before most consonants, frequently unvoicing or spirantalizing the following consonant in the process.

Based on the example M > Ilk. (Ety/BES), it seems that [sn] became [nn] in Ilkorin, as was also the case in Old Noldorin. It is unclear whether such assimilation also occurred for [s] followed by [m], [l] and [r], as happened in Welsh (WGHC/95ii) and Old Noldorin.

The voiceless dental stop survived initially from Primitive Elvish into Ilkorin (PE19/18), but it became [d] after vowels (PE19/23) and became [] (th) after liquids and voiceless stops. It was preserved medially in some clusters, notably [st] and sometimes (final) [nt], though primitive medial [nt] became [nd].

The voiceless dental spirant mainly developed from the primitive aspirate [th] (PE19/18), but medially after vowels it was voiced to [] (PE19/23), and thus [] from primitive [th] appears more often initially than medially.

Another way that [] could develop was from the spirantalization of [t] after liquids and voiceless stops, and thus [] could appear non-finally in clusters such as [r] or [l] (rth or lth). In the case of pairs of primitive voiceless stops, these often reduced to a single [] because . In addition, in the Doriathrin dialect at least, a final [] was again devoiced to [], giving another way for a [] to appear non-initially.

The vowel [u] could be short or long in Ilkorin. Non-final [u] generally survived from Primitive Elvish, except where it underwent a-affection. Short [u] developed from primitive [o] before following [i], a change that was important in the formation of Ilkorin . Long [u] also developed from the primitive diphthong [ou].
The primitive diphthongs [ui] survived in Ilkorin, and also developed from primitive [oi] (PE19/25).

The voiced labial spirant developed from primitive [b] after vowels, and also medially from the voiceless labial spirant [f] (PE19/23), which itself developed from the primitive aspirate [ph]. As such, it could not appear at the beginning of an Ilkorin word. Note that orthographically, a final f represents [v] in Ilkorin as it does in Sindarin.
The semi-vowel [w] mostly survived from Primitive Elvish into Ilkorin, though (PE19/19, 24). The primitive semi-vowel [j] (y) disappeared, either vanishing or become the vowel [i].

A voiceless [w] developed in Ilkorin from the initial clusters [khw], [sw], and [skw] (PE19/20-21). Medially, the cluster [khw] became [h] (PE19/23). Thus, it seems likely this voiceless [w] could only appear initially, but there are no attested examples of Ilkorin words containing this sound.

In Ilkorin, it seems that medial labialized velars were de-labialized, losing the following [w]-sound. There are several examples of this medial development in the Comparative Tables: M-w- > [-gw- >] Ilk. -g-, M-kw- > [-gw- >] Ilk. -g(w)- (PE19/23). There are also a number of examples of this development in The Etymologies (see below). If the [w] in these examples were retained, it would later have become final after , and then this final [w] would have become [u], as happened with M > (Ety/KHIS). The fact that there are no such examples of final [u] after a velar is strong evidence for this de-labialization of medial velars.

According to the Comparative Tables, the development for intervocalic [-xw-] was slightly different. Here, the labialized spirant developed into [-h-], probably first becoming [hw]. This change did not occur if the [-xw-] was preceded by a consonant, in which case the [w] was simply lost, as described above: M > [alxwa >] Ilk. [alx] (Ety/ALAK).

The voiceless velar spirant developed from the primitive aspirate [kh] in Old Ilkorin, but initially the resulting [x] became [h], which unvoiced any following consonant. Medially, the resulting [x] became [h] (perhaps becoming [] first), which then vanished (PE19/23). Thus, primitive aspirates [kh] either vanished from Ilkorin or were pronounced [h] by the time of the wars of Beleriand.

Another way that [x] could develop was from the spirantalization of [k] after liquids and voiceless stops. Thus [x] could appear non-finally in clusters such as [rx] or [lx] (rch or lch). In the case of pairs of primitive voiceless stops [kk], these these reduced to a single [x] because . All attested instances of [x] in Ilkorin were of this origin.

A vowel, probably similar to N. , appearing only in the Ilkorin word . The phonological development of this word is obscure, so it is difficult to say how the vowel [y] developed in Ilkorin, or whether this word was simply an aberration.

In Ilkorin, it seems that [z] vocalized into [i] before voiced stops, similar to developments in Old Noldorin. The clearest examples are M > Ilk. (Ety/MASAG) and M > [miid(e) >] Dor. (Ety/MIZD).

The vocalization after [e] are less clear. There are two examples: M > Ilk. (EtyAC/EZDE) and M > [mezda >] Dor. , where the second example would have developed a medial [-e-] due to Ilkorin a-affection. In these examples, it is possible that the [z] became [e] or simply lengthened the preceding vowel, so that the development was [-ezd-] > [-ed-]. However, the [z] could also have vocalized into [i] as it did after [a] and [i] if the resulting diphthong [ei] became [e] afterwards: [-ezd-] > [-eid-] > [-ed-]. This second development is the theory used here.

There are no attested examples of the vocalization of [z] after [o] and [u] or before [b], but presumably the developments would have been similar, probably resulting in [oi] > [ui] and [ui], respectively.
A notation indicating a vanished sound, used only in phonetic rules.

The Ilkorin word for father derived from primitive Matar[a], also attested in its plural form edrin (Ety/ATA). It is identical to its Noldorin cognate N. having undergone similar phonetic changes from its primitive form, possibly *atara.

A diminutive form of father, similar to English daddy (Ety/ATA). Helge Fauskanger suggested it may have developed from primitive *atto based on its Quenya equivalent MQ. (AL-Ilkorin/adda), but I think that is likelier to be a childs invention, unrelated to other languages.

A Doriathrin word for bridge appearing in the Addenda and Corrigenda to The Etymologies (EtyAC/YAT), likely a derivative of the same primitive form M as its cognates in other languages. An earlier deleted form iaum may indicate Tolkiens uncertainty over the development of initial [j] (= y) in Ilkorin; elsewhere the rule is that .
An Ilkorin word for swan derived from primitive M (Ety/ALAK). This word is a good example of how in Ilkorin.
Ilkorin for mother (Ety/AM1), also appearing in its plural form emnin (EtyAC/AM1).
An Ilkorin prefix meaning outside, beside, the same as in Quenya and Noldorin (Ety/AR2).

A Doriathrin noun meaning the exterior, the outside, literally outside the fence (Ety/GAT(H)). It is a combination of outside and fence. The entry in The Etymologies also had a rejected variant argadon (EtyAC/GAT(H)).
A name for Doriath translated Outside the Fence, a compound of outside the fence (Ety/AT(AT)) and land (Ety/GAT(H), AR2). Thus, its literal meaning is [Land] Outside the Fence.

A variant form of “[Land] Outside the Fence”, marked as in The Etymologies (Ety/GAT(H), Ety/AR²). If so, it is evidence that in that dialect, primitive [g] became [i] between an [r] and a vowel, just as in the main Ilkorin dialect .
conceptualDevelopment: In the Gnomish Lexicon from the 1910s, ᴱIlk. or Ariador was also said to be a dialectical word, from (early) Ilkorin (GL/20), possibly with a similar phonetic development.

descriptionText: A Doriathrin adjective meaning red derived from the root M (Ety/YAR), likely derived from a primitive form such as *yarna [jarna]. It is a good example of how in Ilkorin.
An adjective meaning violent, rushing, impetuous, appearing as the river name (Ety/SKAR).

These developments are similar to those of Old Noldorin. This change for initial or medial aspirates is documented in the Comparative Tables (PE19/18, 21), though the medial developments are obscured because later (PE19/23).
A noun meaning cooked food, meat (Ety/AP). Given its Quenya cognate MQ. , it seems to be an example of how voiceless stops became [s] before [s] in Ilkorin.
A suffix, identical to N. (PE21/57). It is possible this suffix was also used as (and was perhaps inspired by) the Gnomish general plural suffix .

A title in The Etymologies translated Vala-king, a combination of the root M and Ilk. king, also attested in its plural form Balthorin (Ety/BAL). It is an example of how voiceless stops became spirants after liquids l and r.
A noun meaning something like home attested only in compounds like Elvenhome.

This word is marked Ilk. in one entry in The Etymologies (Ety/KOR), but elsewhere the same word is marked as Noldorin: N. (Ety/MBAS). The elements of this word are also marked as Noldorin: N. bread (Ety/MBAS) and N. round (Ety/KOR). It is possible the Ilkorin word underwent the same phonetic development as its Noldorin counterpart, or that it is a loan word from Noldorin.
An Ilkorin word for strength, developed from primitive M (Ety/BEL), an example of how final vowels vanished in Ilkorin.
A noun meaning husband developed from primitive M (Ety/BES), the only example of how in Ilkorin.
A noun meaning valiant man, warrior developed from primitive M (Ety/BER) after the primitive final vowel vanished in Ilkorin.
A rejected noun meaning valor developed from the root M (Ety/BER), perhaps from a primitive form *berette. The word was probably rejected when Elbereth change from an Ilkorin to a Noldorin name.

A word meaning steadfast, trusty man, faithful vassal developed from the primitive form Mboron- (Ety/BOR). Because the initial syllable was stressed in the primitive form, the initial [bor-] did not reduce to [br-] as it did when the primitive vowel was unstressed. The glosses seem to indicate that it could be used as an adjective steadfast or a noun trusty man, faithful vassal. However, it is possible that the first part of the gloss is meant to read steadfast/trusty man, so that the word is only a noun.

A word for mast developed from the primitive form M or *beretha (Ety/BERETH), because in Ilkorin . It seems this word referred to beech nuts rather than the mast of a ship, perhaps generalized to all kinds of forest nuts, as in the Old English word mst. The normal Ilkorin word for beech tree is or .
A word for broken stones, gravel developed from the primitive form M or *biritte (Ety/BIRIT), because in Ilkorin .

A word for bear developed from the primitive form M (Ety/BIRIT), because in Ilkorin , after which the . This word is unusual in that the primitive final vowel did not vanish, but instead developed into -a, as noted by Helge Fauskanger (AL-Ilkorin/broga). The conditions for this exception are unclear, but may have been due to the consonant [g] that developed from primitive [k].

An adjective meaning bowed, bow-shaped, bent developed from the primitive form M (Ety/KU). The middle diphthong went through various sound changes as indicated in The Etymologies. First the [u] became [o] preceding the final [a] (kogna), then the [g] (from ) vocalized to [u] before the [n] (coun) and finally the diphthong [ou] became [au] (caun).
A noun meaning “river” developed from the primitive form ᴹ✶ (Ety/KEL), where the .
conceptualDevelopment: This word was initially marked as Noldorin.

descriptionText: A noun for ship used to in some linguistic notes in the mid-1930s to illustrate the : ciriath. Tolkien first wrote these forms with a short vowel (cir, ciriath), and he vacillated on whether these were Noldorin or Ilkorin words, eventually deciding they were from both languages (PE21/57 noted #28). The proper etymology of the Ilkorin form is unclear; based on the example of < *gwenya we might expect Ilk. **cere instead.

Ilkorin had a class-plural suffix , identical in form and origin to (PE21/57). This suffix appeared in The Etymologies from the 1930s within the collective form Eglath of Elf, both as Doriathrin (Ety/ELED) and general Ilkorin (Ety/GAT(H), LED). It is possible this suffix was also used as (and was perhaps inspired by) the Gnomish general plural suffix .

A noun meaning “sickness” (Ety/KWAM). Its Quenya cognate ᴹQ. indicates a primitive form *✶kwāmē, so this word is an example of how initial [kwo] became [ko] after the primitive vowel [ā] became [ō]. Both these developments were noted by Helge Fauskanger (AL-Ilkorin/côm).
conceptualDevelopment: This word is nearly identical to earlier Gnomish “disease, illness” before Tolkien revised the phonological history of the Noldorin language so that [kw] became [p].

descriptionText:
Tolkien introduced the Ilkorindi towards the end of the Lost Tales (LT2/9), but in this early period they seem to have filled a role more like the later Avari, as a general term for the Elves who did not to go to Valinor. In writings on Early Qenya Phonology from the 1920s, Tolkien described Ilkorin as a family of mutually unintelligible languages (PE14/62). This earlier conception is discussed seperately, as the Early Ilkorin language(s).

In the Lhammas of the 1930s, Tolkien made a point to group the Ilkorins with the other Eldar, distinct from the Lembi who refused to go to Valinor (LR/171). At this stage the term specifically referred to the languages of the Elves of Beleriand, and these languages were closely related, more like dialects of the same language (LR/175).

Later, Tolkien reformed the Noldorin language into Sindarin, designating it as the language of the Elves of Beleriand (WJ/5). At this point he seems to have abandoned the Ilkorin language, but as suggested by Edward Kloczko (Tyalie Tyelellieva #9), Tolkien seems to have recycled some of its phonetic characteristics in the North Sindarin dialect. This let Tolkien retain some of his earlier Ilkorin-based names in his later writings by recasting them as North Sindarin, for example NS. .

A noun meaning small gull, petrel, sea-bird derived from primitive M (EtyAC/KW, PE22/32), an example of how primitive in Ilkorin. In the Etymologies, this word was marked as Ilkorin (EtyAC/KW), while in Tolkiens description of the Feanorian Alphabet, it was marked as Falathrin (PE22/32).
A Doriathrin noun meaning “Elf” derived from primitive ᴹ✶ (EtyAC/KWEN(ED)), an example of the Ilkorin syncope.
conceptualDevelopment: This word is nearly identical to earlier Gnomish “Elf” before Tolkien revised the phonological history of the Noldorin language so that [kw] became [p].

descriptionText: A noun meaning down (feathers) derived from primitive M (Ety/KWES) when the primitive final vowel was lost.

A Doriathrin noun meaning narrator derived from primitive M (Ety/KWET). This word underwent several notable phonetic changes: first the voiceless stop was voiced after the nasal ([nt] > [nd]), after which [e] became [i] before the [nd] ([end] > [ind]) and finally an [o] developed between the consonant and the final [r] ([-dr] > [-dor]). These changes were all noted by Helge Fauskanger (AL-Doriathrin/cwindor).

A noun meaning shadow of trees, derived from root M shadow and marked as identical in both the Ilkorin and Doriathrin dialects (Ety/DAY). Its primitive form was probably *dair- ending in some final vowel, now lost; Helge Fauskanger suggested it might be *daire (AL-Ilkorin/dair, AL-Doriathrin/dair).

A noun meaning night-time, gloom, derived from root M (Ety/DO). The development of its Noldorin and Quenya cognates point to a primitive form of M [dome] (Ety/DO, DOMO). This word probably underwent development similar to its Noldorin cognate N. but with the retention of the final [-m]: dome > dogme > doume > Ilk. daum. The word Ilk. has an attested development that also follows this pattern (Ety/KU). Helge Fauskanger suggested this same phonological history in his study of Ilkorin (Al-Ilkorin/daum).
Doriathrin name for the leader of the Danians (LR/188), called in their own language Dan. (Ety/DAN). This name developed from the primitive form ᴹ✶.
conceptualDevelopment: In Silmarillion drafts from the 1930s, this name first appeared in forms resembling the Doriathrin name: Denilos or Denithor (SM/271). Later in these drafts, it was change to its Danian form Denethor (LR/119, 145). It kept that form thereafter.

descriptionText:
Ilkorin had several distinct dialects. Tolkien mentioned two by name: Falathrin or Falassian spoken by the Elves of the havens of and Doriathrin spoken by the subjects of Thingol in (LR/170, 175). Tolkien also sometimes used the term Beleriandic, but this seems to have simply been a term for the languages of Beleriand in general rather than a specific dialect.

Tolkien designated quite a few words as simply Ilkorin (Ilk.). It is unclear whether these represented a third dialect spoken by Beleriandic Elves outside the two regions mentioned, or whether it was simply a term for words common among all dialects. If it was a distinct dialect, it probably belonged to the other scattered companies of the Ilkorindi that wandered in the land, but these have all perished (LR/175), so that only the Falathrin and Doriathrin dialects survived the fall of Beleriand (LR/178). For purposes of discussion, generic Ilkorin is treated as its own dialect here.
A hypothetical name for the river N. , what the Ilkorin name would have been if it had been derived from the root M (Ety/GYEL). It is an illustration of the rule that in Ilkorin.

A noun that, together with its variant dang, was glossed sound (Ety/DING). Given that its root form M was said to be onomatopoeic, it was probably a word for a particular kind of sound, perhaps like English twang, which is a gloss of several derivatives of the similar root M.

Ilkorin diphthongs were usually survivals or developments from primitive diphthongs, though they could also arise from the the vocalization of [g] before nasals and from the the vocalization of [z] before voiced stops.

An Ilkorin noun for head attested only as an element in the name Wet Head (Ety/MIZD, NDOL). It might also appear in , assuming that name is Ilkorin. Assuming it functions similarly to its Noldorin equivalent N. , it can probably also be used to refer to a hill.
A noun glossed flat, lowlying vale (Ety/DAL). Helge Fauskanger pointed out that the gloss is ambiguous, and it may be that this word can also be used an adjective flat (AL-Ilkorin/dol).

A Doriathrin word for back explicitly marked as a noun (Ety/NDAN). Its primitive form might have been *ndan, so that the primitive long [a] became [o] and the initial nasal [n] was lost before the stop (as suggested by Helge Fauskanger, AL-Doriathrin/don).
A Doriathrin noun for land (EtyAC/NDOR) apparently from primitive M (Ety/NDOR). If its primitive form indeed had a short [o], then this word may be an example of how in Ilkorin.

Doriathrin was the dialect of Ilkorin spoken by the Elves of (LR/175). In The Etymologies, Tolkien marked almost as many words as Doriathrin (Dor.) as he did Ilkorin (Ilk.). There are very few examples of words appearing in both dialects, however, and almost all of them have the same form. In fact, the only words with distinct Ilkorian and Doriathrin forms are the names Ilk. Argad/Argador (Ety/AR2) versus Dor. (Ety/GAT(H)), and Ilk. (Ety/MAP) versus Dor. (Ety/KAB).

Despite the lack of evidence, the examples in The Etymologies do hint at several possible differences between the two dialects:

  • There are a number of Ilkorin words for which final [u] became [o], but there are several Doriathrin words where this does not occur: Dor. , Dor. and Dor. . An exception is Dor. which does seem to have this change.
  • There are a couple of examples in which in Doriathrin, but this change did not occur in the Ilkorin words Ilk. and Ilk. .
  • There are no examples of Ilkorin i-affection in Doriathrin even in cases where it should occur, whereas there are plenty examples of such changes in the plurals of Ilkorin nouns.
  • According to one note (Ety/NAUK), the genitive generally preceded the modified noun in the Doriathrin dialect, such as Dor. . There are several counter-examples in Ilkorin such as Ilk. and Ilk. .

Like Falathrin, the Doriathrin dialect influenced the common language of the survivors of the wars of Beleriand spoken at the mouth of the Sirion river (LR/178).

A Doriathrin noun meaning oak derived from the primitive form Mdoron[o] (Ety/DORON). The accent mark in the root indicated that the first syllable was stressed, thereby preventing the initial [dor-] from becoming [dr-]. The second [o] was lost, however, due to the Ilkorin syncope.

It appears that in Ilkorin, double spirants reduced to single spirants. The clearest example of this is M > [brie >] Ilk. [bri] (Ety/BIRIT). Another possible example is M > [takka > taxxa >] Ilk. [tax] (Ety/TAK) as suggested by Helge Fauskanger (AL-Ilkorin/tach). In the case of primitive [kt] or [kth], it seems the development was to [x] and then [], for example: M > [oxa >] Ilk. (Ety/OKTA). There are no examples of the development for other spirant pairs, but perhaps the preceding spirant assimilated to the following one as a general rule. If so, the assimilation could also have occurred earlier, when the sounds were still stops (as suggested by Helge Fausganger, AL-Ilkorin/oth).

A Doriathrin noun meaning wolf derived from the primitive form M (Ety/DARAK), probably from older *daraka. The accent mark in the root MDARAK indicated that the first syllable was unstressed, so that the initial [dar-] became [dr-]. Thereafter the long [a], became [o] and the voiceless stop [k] voiced to [g] after the vowel.
A noun meaning river, simply an elaboration of its root M (Ety/DUI).
A noun meaning water, river, simply an elaboration of its root M (Ety/DUI).
A noun for twilight developed from primitive M (Ety/DOMO), where the long .

A Doriathrin adjective meaning black (Ety/DUN). Its Noldorin and Danian cognates imply development from a primitive form *dunna. Since the primitive form ended in [a], the Ilkorin a-affection would ordinarily have produced **donn. However, it seems that a-affection was prevented or reversed before [nn], as suggested by Helge Fauskanger (AL-Doriathrin/dunn).

A Doriathrin noun for “sorcery” (Ety/ÑGOL). The elements of this word seem to be a combination of derivatives of the roots ᴹ√ and ᴹ√. If it were derived from such a primitive form, it would imply that in its phonological history the [o] because [u] in both syllables. This does not seem to be a general rule in Ilkorin, however: compare Ilk. and . A simpler explanation would be that it was a loan word from Noldorin: N. seen in a marginal note (EtyAC/ÑGOL).
conceptualDevelopment: There is a rejected form dûghol in this entry of The Etymologies that may represent Tolkien’s first attempt to formulate a native Ilkorin word for “sorcery” (EtyAC/ÑGOL). Similar forms appear among the precursors to S. in Lord of the Rings drafts from the 1940s: Dol Dúgol or (TI/178; WR/122). The entry also has a deleted variant form of gûl of Ilk. , so it may be Tolkien originally envisioned a different phonological history of [o] in Ilkorin allowing the production of words like durgul. Perhaps he added the Noldorin form durgul in the margin because he abandoned [o] > [u] in Ilkorin.

descriptionText: The Ilkorin name of MQ. , developed from the same primitive form M (EtyAC/EZDE).
A Doriathrin noun meaning star, a simple derivative of the root M (Ety/EL).

A rejected Doriathrin word for Elf, a derivation of the root M and a direct cognate of MQ. , also appearing in its plural form Eldin (Ety/ELED). It was replaced by Ilk. derived from the inverted form of the root: Medel[a].

An adjectival suffix appearing as both -en and -in, and in one place as -on: . The -en form can be easily explained as a derivative of the primitive suffix M, with the primitive [i] becoming [e] due to Ilkorin a-affection, the same origin as the Noldorin adjectival suffix . The -in variant is more difficult to explain. At least one example had variations with both -en and -in, so perhaps the two forms represented vacillation on the function of Ilkorin a-affection, or an alternate primitive form M-ina where the final a was lost before a-affection.

Alternately, -in could be a Doriathrin-specific variant, since the forms where it appears are all Doriathrin, while the forms where -en appear are marked Ilkorin, excepting only lomen which was itself revised from lomin.
The Ilkorin word for one attested only in the name or Ermab(r)in One-handed (Ety/MAP).
A noun meaning seed, germ derived from primitive M (Ety/ERED). The middle [e] was lost due to the Ilkorin syncope, and afterwards the , as suggested by Helge Fauskanger (AL-Ilkorin/erdh).

A noun meaning sedge derived from the root M (Ety/ESEK), probably from a primitive form *eseke. The middle [e] was lost due to the Ilkorin syncope, and afterwards the , as suggested by Helge Fauskanger (AL-Ilkorin/esg).

A rejected noun meaning rustle, noise of leaves derived from the root M (Ety/EZGE). Its (rejected) Quenya cognate MQ. indicates a primitive form *eseke, despite the root form. If so, middle [e] was lost due to the Ilkorin syncope, and afterwards the .
A noun for wound derived from the root M (Ety/SKAR). Apparently the initial [sk-] became syllabic [sk-], which then became [esk-]. Afterwards the .

A noun for reed-bed, apparently an elaboration of Ilk. reed (Ety/ESEK). In a hastily written entry in The Etymologies, a similar form esgar was glossed shore as a derivative of the root M, but with no language specified (EtyAC/SKAR2). If it was Ilkorin, it probably underwent the same development as wound. Both these words appeared to have been coined to explain the name of the town from the Hobbit.

A noun derived from the root MSPALAS and glossed foaming (?fall); the second word in the gloss is unclear (Ety/PHAL). It was marked as Ilkorin (EtyAC/PHAL). Apparently the initial [sp-] became syllabic [sp-] and then became [esp-].

Falathrin, also referred to as Falassian, was the dialect of Ilkorin spoken by the Elves of the havens of and (LR/175). There are only three attested words specifically designated as Falathrin: which is identical in form to its Doriathin equivalent (Ety/BERETH), a sea bird also identical to its Ilkorin equivalent (EtyAC/KW, PE22/32), and finally , a Falathrin variant of (Ety/GAT(H), AR2). This last example hints that perhaps primitive [g] became [i] between an [r] and a vowel in Falathrin, whereas in the main Ilkorin dialect this change only occurred for [g] between [l] and a vowel. The Falassian dialect influenced the common language of the survivors of the wars of Beleriand spoken at the mouth of the Sirion river (LR/178).

In Doriathrin it seems that a final [] (= dh) became [] (= th); a similar development occurred in Gnomish. The clearest example of this change is M > rodh > Dor. roth (Ety/ROD).

A more complex example is Dor. , whose cognates N. and MQ. imply a primitive form of [arda] or [garda] (Ety/AR). This means that first the , and then developed into [] when it became final after the loss of the vowel. This change is more clearly indicated by the deleted Doriathrin form: garth (dh) (EtyAC/ARA). Helge Fauskanger also suggested this development (AL-Doriathrin/garth).

There are a few examples where this change did not occur: Ilk. and Ilk. . It may be that this change only occurred in the Doriathrin dialect.

Where [j] (y) or [w] became final after , these final [j], [w] first became [i], [u], then the resulting [i] and [u] became [e] and [o] in most cases. The clearest examples of this development are Mwinya > gwini > Ilk. (Ety/WIN) and M > gwelu > Ilk. (Ety/WIL). This changed did not occur where the final vowel was part of a diphthong: (Ety/WA).

There are a several examples where this change did not occur in the case of [-u]: Dor. , Dor. and Dor. . All of these examples were marked Doriathrin in The Etymologies, so perhaps this development did not occur in that dialect of Ilkorin, though it does seem to have occurred with Dor. magic, lore (Ety/NGOL).

Where [j] (y) or [w] became final after , these semi-vowels became vowels, first becoming [i] and [u], after which these . The clearest examples of this development are Mwinya > gwini > Ilk. (Ety/WIN) and M > gwelu > Ilk. (Ety/WIL).

In Ilkorin, it seems that final [-mb] and [-mm] reduced to [-m], the former probably developing as [-mb] > [-mm] > [-m]. The clearest example of this change is M > trumb > Ilk. (Ety/TURUM). A similar changed occurred in Noldorin, but unlike Noldorin, this change did not occur medially in Ilkorin, as indicated by Ilk. .

In Ilkorin, it seems that final [-nd] and [-ll] reduced to [-n] and [-l], but only in polysyllables; there are several examples where these sounds are preserved in monosyllables. The clearest example of this change is M > ulgund > ulgon > Ilk. (Ety/ULUG). Another likely example is M > [gandell(e) >] Ilk. , as indicated by its cognate MQ. (Ety/NGAN). Final [-nd] probably developed as [-nd] > [-nn] > [-n], and the same change probably applied to final [-nn], but there are no clear examples of these developments.

It seems that in Ilkorin, a final [-un] developed into [-on]. The clearest example is M > Ilk. (Ety/KEL). This change can also be seen in M > ulgund > ulgon > Ilk. (Ety/ULUG). Both these developments were noted by Helge Fauskanger (AL-Ilkorin/celon, ulgund). This change may be related to the syllabic development of final [n], in which a final [n] preceded by a consonant developed into [-on].

A Doriathrin noun meaning fence derived from the root M (Ety/GAT(H)), most likely from a primitive form *gat-. As pointed out by Helge Fauskanger (AL-Doriathrin/gad), its gloss is a bit peculiar, given that the other derivatives of its root same to have meanings associated with caves. As Mr. Fauskanger suggested, this may represent a transition in Tolkiens thinking on the meaning of the associated name : Land of the Cave (Ety/GAT(H)) >> Land of the Fence (WJ/370).

A Doriathrin (and Falathrin) noun for beech (tree), a combination of tree and (beech) mast (Ety/GALAD, BERETH). The second element originally meant beech, but later meant mast; this original meaning seems to be preserved in this compound.

A Doriathrin noun for tree derived from the root MGALAD (Ety/GALAD), probably from a primitive form *galada with the second a lost due to the Ilkorin Syncope. Note that the first element [gal-] did not reduce to [gl-] because the initial syllable was stressed in the primitive word.

A noun meaning harp derived from the root M (Ety/NGAN), probably from a primitive form *ngandelle based on its Quenya cognate MQ. . Its plural form genglin is a good representation of the rules for in Ilkorin: the suffix , the syncope of the final vowel and mutation of other vowels. It is also an example of how primitive [nd] sometimes became [g] in Ilkorin. As suggested by Helge Fauskanger, this may be due to assimilation to the preceding [g] (AL-Ilkorin/gangel).

A Doriathrin word (noun and adjective?) for a male derived from the root M (Ety/AN).

Possible Etymology: Its Quenya cognate MQ. indicates a primitive form *anu [anu], but ordinarily a primitive final vowel was lost in Ilkorin. Helge Fauskanger suggested that this Ilkorin word was instead derived for adjective form *anwa [anwa], which would have produced final -u after the loss of the [-a] because final [w] became [u]. This derivation is indicated in the Phonetic Developments given below.

An alternate possibility, though, is that [u] was an exception to the rule that final vowels were lost in Ilkorin. The Noldorin development MAN > ON. > N. hints at a similar process. This uncertainly in its etymology makes it difficult to determine the part of speech (noun and/or adjective) that this word belongs to.

A Doriathrin noun for “wolf” derived from the root ᴹ√ÑGAR(A)M (Ety/ÑGARAM), probably from a primitive form *✶ŋgaramō given its Quenya and Noldorin cognates ᴹQ. and N. (as suggested by Helge Fauskanger, AL-Doriathrin/garm). If so, the second a was lost due to the Ilkorin Syncope, and the the initial [ŋg-] simplified to [g-]. The initial syllable of the primitive form was probably stressed, since the initial [ŋgar-] did not simplify to [ŋgr-].
conceptualDevelopment: An earlier version of this entry had the root ᴹ√ƷARAM, but this produced the same form Dor. garm in Doriathrin [Ilkorin] since initial [ɣ] became [g].

descriptionText: A Doriathrin noun for “lord” derived from the root ᴹ√ or possibly ᴹ√GAR (Ety/ƷAR), perhaps from a primitive form *✶ɣarān-. If so, the initial [ɣ] became [g], while the long [ā] became [ō] and then shortened to [o] in the final syllable of a polysyllable.
conceptualDevelopment: An earlier version of this entry had Dor. garan, which likely had a short [a] in the second syllable which was preserved. Since it did not undergo the Ilkorin Syncope, the primitive form likely either had no final vowel or ended in a short [a], so the second [a] was in the final syllable, which seems to have prevented the syncope; this theory is supported by its Quenya cognate ᴹQ. .

descriptionText: An adjective meaning bright derived from the root M, the basis of the river name (Ety/GYEL). There isnt enough information to deduce its primitive form, but Helge Fauskanger suggested *galjana (AL-Ilkorin/gelion), which seems reasonably plausible.
A Doriathrin noun for sky derived from the root M (Ety/EL), probably from a primitive form *elle [elle] based on its cognates. It is a clear example of how initial [] became [g] in Ilkorin.

A Doriathrin adjective meaning (pale) blue derived from the root M (Ety/EL), probably from a primitive form *elwa [elwa] based on its cognates. If so, the initial [] became [g], the primitive final [a] vanished, after which the final [w] became [u]. These developments were noted by Helge Fauskanger (AL-Doriathrin/gelu).

There are a few attested genitive inflections of Ilkorin words in The Etymologies, most of them as elements in compounds. The singular genitive inflections end in the suffix -a and the plural inflections in -ion. Based on the example Dor. naugla (Ety/NAUK), it seems the genitive suffix could cause vowel loss (syncope) just as with . Based on the example Ilk. thurnion (Ety/THOR), the genitive plural could also cause i-affection in the Ilkorin dialect like as well, though not in the Doriathrin dialect: Dor. than thanion (LR/405).

The genitive inflection itself is attested as (Ety/NAUK). According to that entry, the genitive generally preceded the modified noun in the Doriathrin dialect. This rule may have only applied to that dialect, since there are several counter-examples in general Ilkorin: Ilk. and Ilk. . The form -a(n) hints that the genitive might sometimes be expressed with the suffix -n, perhaps after nouns ending in a vowel. If so, this would make the Ilkorin genitive inflection almost the same as the earlier Gnomish , which used -a/-ion after nouns ending in consonants and -n/-thon after nouns ending in vowels (GG/10).

A preposition “from, away” marked as both Ilkorin (Ety/ƷŌ̆; PE21/60) and Doriathrin (EtyAC/ƷŌ̆). It developed from primitive ᴹ✶ʒō̆ (Ety/WŌ), with the initial [ɣ] becoming [g]. It was also used as patronymic, as in go-Thingol “*child of Thingol” (Ety/ƷŌ̆).
conceptualDevelopment: This preposition may be a restoration of the Gnomish patronymic G. .

descriptionText: A noun meaning dirtiness, filth derived from primitive M (Ety/WA). This word underwent quite a few phonetic developments, as indicated below and as described by Helge Fauskanger (AL-Ilkorin/god).

A verb meaning to soil, stain derived from primitive M (Ety/WA). This word underwent quite a few phonetic developments similar to those of related dirtiness, filth, as indicated below and as described by Helge Fauskanger (AL-Ilkorin/goda-).

A (rejected?) Doriathrin noun for light derived from primitive M appearing in The Etymologies (Ety/KAL, EtyAC/KAL). According to Christopher Tolkiens notes, it was part of a rejected etymology for the name , but it isnt clear whether this noun was rejected or if it was just the etymology. Its long primitive vowel [a] became [o] as was the norm in Ilkorin.

A Doriathrin name for the Silmarils, a combination of the genitive form of Noldo and jewel (Ety/MIR, NGOLOD), hence: *Noldo-jewel. It also appeared in the variant form Goldomir, which may hint at the primitive form of the .

An adjective meaning soiled, dirty derived from primitive M [wara] (Ety/WA). This word underwent quite a few phonetic developments, as indicated below and as described by Helge Fauskanger (AL-Ilkorin/gor).

A noun glossed shade (shadow) derived from the root M (Ety/WATH). It is a clear example of how in Ilkorin, and it appears in several names: (Woman of) Secret Shadow and (unglossed but presumably *Mountains of Shadow).
A noun meaning wind derived from the root MWAW(A) (Ety/WA). Here the , and after the final vowel vanished, the final [w] became [u].
A noun meaning bond derived from primitive M (Ety/WED). Here the , and the [d] spirantalized to [].

A noun for “air” or “the lower air”, derived from the same primitive form ᴹ✶ as its Quenya equivalent ᴹQ. Wilwa (Ety/WIL). Here the . Furthermore, after the final [a] was lost, the final [w] became [u] and then became [o], as suggested by Helge Fauskanger (AL-Ilkorin/gwelo).
conceptualDevelopment: In the Addenda and Corrigenda to The Etymologies, Carl Hostetter and Patrick Wynne indicated the Tolkien revised this form to gwelm at the same time as he change its primitive to ᴹ✶wilmā and the Quenya form to ᴹQ. Wilma (EtyAC/WIL). This entry keeps the earlier Ilkorin form gwelo because Tolkien never revised ᴹQ. Wilwa in the narratives of this period.

descriptionText: A noun for girl derived from primitive M (Ety/WEN). Here the .
A noun for greenness derived from the root M (Ety/GWEN).

An adjective for green derived from the root M (Ety/GWEN). Its Quenya cognate MQ. wenya suggests its primitive form was *gwenya [gwenja]. If so, it is an example of how, after final [a] was lost, the final [j] became [i] and then became [e], as suggested by Helge Fauskanger (AL-Ilkorin/gwene).

A noun for butterfly derived from the root M (Ety/GWEN). Its Quenya cognate MQ. wilwarind- suggests its primitive form was *wilwarinde. If so, it is an example of how [nd] sometimes became [g] in Ilkorin. As suggested by Helge Fauskanger, this may be due to assimilation to the preceding [g] (AL-Ilkorin/gwilwering).
An adjective for pale blue derived from the root MGWINDI, rejected along with its root (EtyAC/GWINDI).

A noun for evening derived from primitive Mwinya [winja], but it was rejected along with its root MWIN (Ety/WIN). It is the clearest example of the Ilkorin phonetic development whereby final [j] became [i] and then became [e], since Tolkien indicated the intermediate forms before rejecting the word.
A noun for spindrift, flying spray derived from primitive M (Ety/WIG). Here the .

An archaic prefix meaning together derived from primitive M (Ety/WO). It was lost because it coalesced with the preposition from. As such, it is the clearest example of how initial [gwo] became [go] in Ilkorin.

A Doriathrin adjective for grey written heu in The Etymologies, and derived from the primitive form M [khithwa] (Ety/KHIS). This word illustrates several interesting phonetic changes in Ilkorin.

  1. The [i] became [e] before the final [a].
  2. Both the : [kh-] > [x-] and [-th-] > [--].
    1. Later the .
    2. Meanwhile the medial [--] voiced to [--] (dh).
  3. The primitive final [a] was lost.
  4. Afterwards, the resulting final [w] became [u].

In most other Doriathrin words, a final [u] from [w] further developed into [o]; it is unclear why this change did not occur here.
A noun glossed captain derived from the root M command (EtyAC/KHES). The language of this word is unclear; Carl Hostetter and Patrick Wynne indicated it might be ?Bel. for Beleriandic = Ilkorin.

A Doriathrin noun for fog written hium in The Etymologies, and derived from the primitive form M [khithme] (Ety/KHIS, EtyAC/KHIS). This word illustrates several interesting phonetic changes in Ilkorin.

  1. Both the : [kh-] > [x-] and [-th-] > [--].
    1. Later the .
    2. Meanwhile the medial [--] voiced to [--] (dh).
  2. The primitive final [e] was lost.
  3. Afterwards, the resulting final [m] became syllabic and developed into [-um].
A Doriathrin noun for lady attested only as an element in the name (Ety/NEL). It probably had essentially the same derivation as its Noldorin cognate N. (Ety/KHER).

The Ilkorindi were among the Elves who went on the great journey but chose to remain behind in Beleriand when the rest of their kin left for Valinor (LR/112). After this, the Ilkorin languages diverged from those of the other Eldar. As most of the Ilkorins were members of the third tribe, their languages were originally related to the (Middle) Telerin language spoken by the Sea Elves (LR/175). After the Noldorin exile to Beleriand, the Noldorin and Ilkorin languages strongly influenced one another (LR/177), but judging from the Tree of Tongues (LR/170), Ilkorin had more influence on Noldorin than the other way around. Regardless, many of the later phonetic changes of Noldorin resemble those of Ilkorin. After the fall of Beleriand, it seems that most of the Ilkorindi joined with the Noldor returning to the West, but a few remained behind, slowly fading away under the doom of Mandos (LR/178).
A word for a blow with an axe in Early Noldorin Word-lists of the 1920s derived from primitive Eskanta (PE13/147).
Apparently a feminine suffix attested only in the name (Ety/LUK).
Apparently a feminine suffix attested in the name (Woman of) Secret Shadow (Ety/THUR) and the noun queen (Ety/TA).
A suffix appearing in almost all attested Ilkorin plurals.
conceptualDevelopment: This suffix is the same as the most common Gnomish plural suffix (GG/10).

descriptionText: In Ilkorin an initial [j] (= y) vanished. This change is described in the Comparative Tables (PE19/19) and there are several examples in The Etymologies (see below).

It seems that [w] was lost between an initial [k] or [g] and a following [o]. There is one example of this change for [kwo-]: M > [kwame > kwom(e) >] (Ety/KWAM). For the case of [gwo-], the clearest example is archaic together, for which Tolkien said: in Ilk. owing to coalescence of gwo, o (in go) this prefix was lost (Ety/WO). The other examples of this rule involve an initial [w] becoming [gw], and then a resulting [gwo-] becoming [go-] (see below). This change was suggested by Helge Fauskanger (AL-Ilkorin/god, gor, gwo-).
Based on the example M > Ilk. (Ety/MOROK), it seems that the initial combination [mr-] became [br-] in Ilkorin after the unstressed vowel vanished.
These developments are clearly described on the Comparative Tables (PE19/19). In The Etymologies, there are no examples [ŋ-], but the examples for [ɣ-] are numerous (see below).
conceptualDevelopment: In later notes on the development of Beleriandic [Ilkorin] ʒ and ñ written around 1950, Tolkien first described the same changes as above, but then revised the development of initial [ɣ-] to become [h-] (PE18/103-4, note #148). There are no attested examples of this revised development, however, and Tolkien abandoned the Ilkorin/Beleriandic language soon after these notes were written.

descriptionText:
This Ilkorin phonetic rule is similar to sound changes that occurred in Old Noldorin. The likely development was that the stops first became aspirates [ph], [th] and [kh], after which the initial [s] was lost and then the [f-], [-] and [x-] (> [h-]), as indicated on the Comparative Tables (PE19/20). In The Etymologies, the only attested examples of this rule involve [st-] > [-] (see below).

This change did not occur where the initial [s] became syllabic: compare MSPALAS > Ilk. (Ety/PHAL).

This Ilkorin phonetic rule is similar to sound changes that occurred in later Old Sindarin but not in contemporaneous Old Noldorin. Afterwards, the initial [s] was lost to leave only the voiceless initial consonants, as indicated on the Comparative Tables (PE19/20). There are no attested examples of this development in The Etymologies.
conceptualDevelopment: In later linguistic notes from around 1950, the “Beleriandic” development seems to have been initial [s-] to [θ-] instead: “sr > thr (þr)” (PE18/94), whereas simple initial y, w, l, r always became unvoiced (PE18/105). Both these developments were similar to the rules of Old Noldorin and Noldorin, so perhaps Tolkien switched the phonetic rules between the two languages; the later Sindarin language had the same development as the Ilkorin of the 1930s. This revision occurred shortly before Tolkien abandoned the Ilkorin language entirely.

descriptionText: This rule is described on the Comparative Tables along with the unvoicing effects of the initial [s] (PE19/20-21), but in The Etymologies the only examples are [st-] > [-] (see below).
In Ilkorin an initial [w] became [gw], as was also the case in Noldorin. This change is described in the Comparative Tables (PE19/19) and there are numerous examples in The Etymologies (see below).

In the Comparative Tables, an initial aspirate [kh] developed into [h] (PE19/18). This was also true when the aspirate developed from an initial [s]: Msk > [kh >] Ilk. h (PE19/20). There are several examples of this development in The Etymologies (see below).

In the Comparative Tables, where the initial aspirate [kh] appeared before an [l], [r], [w], the result was a voiceless [l], [r], [w] (PE19/18, 21). This was also true when the aspirate developed from an initial [s]: Mskw > [khw >] Ilk. hw (PE19/20). There is only one example of this rule in The Etymologies: M > Dor. (EtyAC/KHARAS).

Most likely this development occurred after , ([kh-] > [x-]), and was part of the general trend whereby . This development did not occur for [j] (y), since either [j] was lost after initial velars or ; Tolkien vacillated on the exact development of [j] after initial velars.

translatedWord: initial nasals usually vanished before stops
transliteratedWord: initial nasals usually vanished before stops
pronunciationText: initial nasals usually vanished before stops
descriptionText:
The Comparative Tables indicate that primitive initial combinations of nasals and voiced stops generally lost their nasal sound (PE19/20). The same rule applied to Beleriandic development in Tolkiens linguistic notes from around 1950 (PE18/103-4). There are a number of examples of this development in The Etymologies (see below).

However, the actual development in the Comparative Tables shows mb > Ilk. b, mb; nd > Ilk. d, nd; ng > Ilk. g, ng. This indicates that while the normal development was to simple stops, in some case the development could be different. There are a number of examples of such alternate development in The Etymologies. The Doriathrin derivatives of the root M all show variations beginning with both g- and ng-, while the Doriathrin derivatives M all begin with ng-. Similarly, M > Dor. , with a simple nasal instead of a simple stop.

All the examples of this variation are Doriathrin and occur before the vowel [o]. There is an example of a Doriathrin noun with [g-] > [g-] before [a], however: M > Dor. . Furthermore, there are no examples of this variation for [nd-], whereas M > Dor. . Therefore the conditions of this variant development may be where [mb-] and [g-] precede the vowel be [o] (and perhaps [u]) and the variation may be limited to the Doriathrin dialect.

In the case of [mb-], it seems the variation leads to the simple nasal [m-]. It may be that ng- is an orthographic representation of the simple velar nasal [-], so that in both cases the nasal-stop cluster reduced to a simple nasal for the variation.

In the Ilkorin phonetic developments described in The Etymologies, it appears that an initial palatalized velar became a non-palatalized dental, as noted by Helge Fauskanger (AL-Ilkorin/telf), similar to the medial development of labialized velars described in the Comparative Tables (PE19/23). There are two examples: Ilk. derived from the root ᴹ√ (Ety/GYEL) and Ilk. derived from the root ᴹ√ (Ety/KYELEP). It seems likely the rule applied to other initial labialized velars as well.
conceptualDevelopment: This rule contradicts the initial developments described in the Comparative Tables, where [j] was lost after initial velars (PE19/18-20). It seems that Tolkien changed his mind between writing the tables and beginning work on The Etymologies. In some later tables on “Belariandric”, it seems Tolkien toyed with restoring this development (PE18/105): gy > g (not d), but he soon after abandoned the Ilkorin language completely.

translatedWord: [j] was lost after initial velars and dentals
transliteratedWord: [j] was lost after initial velars and dentals
pronunciationText: [j] was lost after initial velars and dentals
descriptionText: In the Ilkorin phonetic developments described in the Comparative Tables, initial labialized velar lost their labialization but remained velars (PE19/18-20), and similarly for dentals (PE19/22). This change is not attested in The Etymologies, where it seems that .
The Doriathrin word for the Moon developed from the primitive name M (Ety/I2), though it is unclear how the [st] developed. Perhap it was of the same origin as silver light, starlight (Ety/SIL).

A Doriathrin noun for silver light, starlight, also given as istel, which developed from the root M (Ety/SIL). Tolkien said that it was probably originally a (ancient?) Quenya word learned from Melian. This apparently this means its development was unusual. Along with the identical Moon, it is the only Ilkorin noun with a medial [st]. Helge Fauskanger suggested it must have developed by a strengthening of [s] to [st]. It may also be another example of a development from syllabic [s], though elsewhere .
A rejected Doriathrin noun for babe developed from the root M (EtyAC/LAP). Its Quenya cognate MQ. suggests a primitive form of *lapse, but elsewhere a medial [ps] became [ss] in Ilkorin, as with < M.

An adjective meaning fresh, lively developed from the primitive form M (Ety/LAYAK). It is a good example of how in Ilkorin, as suggested by Helge Fauskanger (AL-Ilkorin/laig). This allowed it to blend with the derivative of M and assume the additional meanings keen, sharp (Ety/LAIK).

A noun meaning elm-tree developed from the root M (Ety/ALAM). An identical form appeared elsewhere in The Etymologies with its language marked D, perhaps for Doriathrin (Ety/LALAM). This word is unusual in that its final [m] did not become syllabic after a consonant, although it did for other similar words such as .

Where the diphthongs [ei] and [ou] developed at a later stage in Ilkorin, from the vocalization of [z] or of [g], these diphthongs developed into [e] and [ou], as opposed to primitive M[ei] and M[ou] which became [i] and [u] respectively (PE19/25). The development is well-attested for [ou] > [au]: M > kogna > coun > Ilk. (Ety/KU). This rule is more speculative in the case of [ei] > [e], but can be deduced from examples like M > Ilk. (EtyAC/EZDE). Helge Fauskanger suggested instead that this might simply be due to the lengthening of the original [e] rather than the development of a diphthong [ei] (AL-Doriathrin/med).

englishWord: licking up (food or drink), gluttonous eating

descriptionText: A Doriathrin noun for gold developed from primitive M, properly golden light rather than the metal (Ety/LAWAR).

An adjective meaning tuneful, sweet developed from primitive M (Ety/LIND, EtyAC/LIND). It is an example of how the usual Ilkorin a-affection was prevented or reverted before [nd], as suggested by Helge Fauskanger (AL-Ilkorin/lind). This word may also have had the sense *singing in the word nightingale = *night singing, from primitive M.

A noun for pool derived from the root M (Ety/LIN1). Its Quenya cognate MQ. suggests its primitive form was *linya [linja]. If so, it is an example of how, after final [a] was lost, the final [j] became [i] and then became [e], as suggested by Helge Fauskanger (AL-Ilkorin/line).
A Doriathrin noun for “fish” derived from primitive ᴹ✶ (Ety/LIW). It is the clearest example of how , as suggested by Helge Fauskanger (AL-Doriathrin/líw). @@@ same development in ᴱN hiw PE13/147
conceptualDevelopment: This word first appeared as rejected ling (EtyAC/LIW), probably reflecting Tolkien’s uncertainty on the development of [-ŋgw-] in Ilkorin.

descriptionText: Ilkorin name of N. , from which the Noldorin name was derived (Ety/LAM). It is a combination of echoing and land.
Ilkorin name of N. , from which the Noldorin name was derived (Ety/LAM). It is a combination of echoing and the plural of mountain.

This phonetic change is common to all Eldarin languages and is very well attested. Most likely this was a parallel change rather than a change taking place in Common Eldarin; there is evidence that it occurred later in Quenya @@@. This change is sufficiently common that it is omitted from the etymologies of Ilkorin words unless it is explicitly documented.

transliteratedWord: long vowels shortened in final syllables
pronunciationText: long vowels shortened in final syllables
descriptionText: There are several clear examples of Ilkorin words that had long vowels in what would eventually become its final syllable, but the vowel is short in the Ilkorin word: M > Dor. Luthien (Ety/LUK) and M > Dor. (LR/188). There are also no Ilkorin polysyllables with long vowels in the final syllable. The likeliest explanation was that long vowels were shortened in final syllables. The rule also seems to apply to compounds, such as Ilk. Wet Head = + (Ety/MIZD).

An adjective meaning empty attested only as an element in the Ilkorin name (Ety/MAP). As suggested by Helge Fauskanger, it might be a combination of Dor. and the adjective suffix , but if so it is unclear where the medial g came from (AL-Ilkorin/Mablosgen). Alternately, perhaps losgen is the general Ilkorin adjective for empty and lost is a variant used only in the Doriathrin dialect.

A Doriathrin adjective meaning empty attested only as an element in the name Dor. (Ety/KAB). Its Quenya cognate suggests a primitive form *lusta, with the [o] developing from Ilkorin a-affection. It might be a Doriathrin-only variant of more general Ilkorin empty.

A Doriathrin adjective for pale derived from primitive M, a revision of the form luin that appeared in The Etymologies as published in The Lost Road (Ety/LUG2, EtyAC/LUG2). The revision of [ui] >> [u] probably reflects Tolkiens vacillation on how primitive in Ilkorin. The earlier form of this word might an element in the name Werewolf (LR/134), which in earlier writings was glossed Werewolf Pale (LB/205). The early Noldorin word EN. pale might be a precursor to it (PE13/149).

A Doriathrin adjective for heavy derived from primitive M (Ety/LUG1). It is an example of how the Ilkorin a-affection was prevented or reverted before [g], as suggested by Helge Fauskanger (AL-Doriathrin/lung).

An unglossed Doriathrin word derived from the root M magic, enchantment appearing as an element in the name Enchantress (Ety/LUK). Since it ends in -th [], it probably developed from a primitive form such as *lukte, as suggested by Helge Fauskanger (AL-Doriathrin/luth). This primitive form is likely the basis for its Noldorin cognate N. spell, charm as well, so the Doriathrin word probably has a similar meaning. The primitive [kt] would have developed into [x] when double voiceless stops became spirants and this simplified to [] when . There was a similar development for < M.

An Ilkorin and Doriathrin noun for hand derived from primitive M (Ety/MAP, EtyAC/MAP), where the voiceless stop [p] voiced to [b] after the vowel. Since its primitive form had a short [a] and its Ilkorin form a long [a] (EtyAC/MAP), this word is an example of how in Ilkorin.
A rejected Ilkorin name from The Etymologies from the 1930s, possibly a variation of Ilk. (EtyAC/LUY). It seems to be a combination of hand and the rejected form luin of pale.
A noun for dough derived from primitive M (Ety/MASAG), where the primitive , as suggested by Helge Fauskanger (AL-Ilkorin/maig).

An adjective meaning soft, pliant derived from primitive M (EtyAC/MASAG). It had essentially the same development as the noun dough (from M), because in both cases the primitive final vowel vanished without further effect.

As indicated in the Comparative Tables, medial [j] (= y) became [i] in Ilkorin (PE19/23). There are no clear examples of this development in The Etymologies, though there are several examples where final [j] became [i]. Helge Fauskanger suggested that the primitive form of bright might be *galjana (AL-Ilkorin/gelion); if so, it would be an example of this medial development.

descriptionText: According to the sound changes in the Comparative Tables, it seems that medial labialized velars became non-labialized dentals in Ilkorin: see below (PE19/23). There are no attested examples of this development in The Etymologies, though compare and where this change seems to have occurred initially. In general the [j] was lost after dentalization, but after primitive [kh] > [x] > [], the [j] became [i] (and then the [] became []).

transliteratedWord: medial voiceless spirants voiced after vowels
pronunciationText: medial voiceless spirants voiced after vowels
descriptionText:
This rule is implied by the Comparative Tables, where medial aspirates became voiced spirants (PE19/23). Since at first , this means those medial voiceless spirant must later have become voiced. The examples in The Etymologies indicate this change occurred medially after vowels (Dor. ), but not after consonants (Ilk. ) or finally (Ilk. ).

In the Comparative Tables, the medial development for the aspirate [kh] is somewhat obscure, given as kh > h > - (PE19/23). Since medial [h] did not disappear when it developed from khw, I think the likeliest explanation is that the velar [x] that developed from [kh] first voiced to [], after which the .

There are numerous examples of final unvoiced spirants in Ilkorin, such as < M. This implies that the medial voicing occurred after primitive final vowels vanished. It cannot be the case that final spirants later lost their voicing, since there are also examples of final voiced spirants, such as < M.

There are a number of names that are possible counter-examples to this rule: Ilk. , Dor. , Dor. and Ilk. . Most of these can be explained as later compounds, but the last is given an explicit primitive form M [ndanitharo] and cognates in other languages (LR/188). This name does not appear in The Etymologies, so perhaps Tolkien was thinking of another phonetic scenario when this name was coined.

Helge Fauskanger (writing before the Comparative Tables were published) suggested an alternate theory: that the medial voicing did not occur between vowels, but only before certain consonants (AL-Doriathrin/hedhu). The two clear examples of this change showed this development only before [w] and [m], so perhaps in between writing the Comparative Tables and The Etymologies, Tolkien decided that the medial voicing only occurred before labials or some similar scenario.

transliteratedWord: medial voiceless stops, nasals and [ɣ] became [s] before [s]

descriptionText: For voiceless stops, this rule can be deduced from examples in The Etymologies: M > Ilk. (Ety/TUP), M > Ilk. (Ety/TAK) and M > [natse >] Dor. (Ety/NAT), the last example implied by its cognate MQ. . For the nasals and [], the rule is described in Tolkiens late notes on the development of Beleriandic [Ilkorin] and n, where he stated that medial ns > ns > ss; s > ss (PE18/104), though there are no attested examples of these changes. The development of [ms] is unclear, but it may have become [ss] as well.

transliteratedWord: medial voiceless stops were voiced after nasals

descriptionText: This rule is a counterpart to the rule that . There are two examples of this rule: M > Dor. (Ety/KWET) and M > Ilk. (Ety/TAK). There are no examples of this rule for [mp], but it may also have applied to this combination. Helge Fauskanger noted these developments in his analysis, and hypothesized that it might apply to Ilk. as well (AL-Doriathrin/cwindor; AL-Ilkorin/tangol, tingla-). It seems that this change did not occur finally or in later compounds: Ilk. or Ilk. .

A Doriathrin noun for moisture derived from primitive M (Ety/MIZD). The [i] lengthened due to the vocalization of [z] before voiced stops, as suggested by Helge Fauskanger (AL-Doriathrin/mid). According to Carl Hostetter and Patrick Wynne, this form was originally unglossed and may have been initially intended to mean fine rain like its Quenya cognate MQ. (EtyAC/MIZD, VTE/45).
A word for jewel attested only in compounds, probably of the same derivation and meaning as its Noldorin cognate N. .
A rejected and hard-to-analyze Ilkorin name for the Silmarils appearing in The Etymologies from the 1930s, revised to N. (EtyAC/MIR). It seems to contain jewel.
A noun for night derived from primitive M (EtyAC/MOR), where the primitive [o] became [o].

A Doriathrin noun for sorcery, written as mor(n)gul indicating the loss of an earlier n (Ety/NGOL). The elements of this word seem to be a combination of derivatives of the roots M and M. The u in the final element -gul is problematic phonetically, as it is in the similar word . Tolkien first wrote this word as morgol (EtyAC/NGOL), probably reflecting this phonetic uncertainty. As with , Tolkien may have resolved this uncertainty by deciding this word was Noldorin, since N. appears in a marginal note in The Etymologies (EtyAC/NGOL).

A Doriathrin noun for pool, derived from root M (Ety/MBOTH). Its Quenya cognate MQ. suggests a primitive form of *mbottho. As pointed out by Helge Fauskanger (AL-Doriathrin/moth), the primitive [mb-] might be expected to have become [b-], since in Ilkorin, as for example Ilk. < MBIRIL.
A Doriathrin adjective meaning secret, veiled derived from root M (Ety/MUY), apparently a combination of vagueness and the adjective-suffix -in.

The Ilkorin noun for nightingale, appearing as both murilind and myrilind (Ety/MOR, TIN). Its Quenya cognate MQ. indicates a primitive form of *morilinde, further supported by the rejected Ilkorin form morilind (EtyAC/MOR). This would have produced murilind according to the rules of Ilkorin i-affection. The variant form myrilind hints at a different (dialectical?) phonetic development, as pointed out by Helge Fauskanger (AL-Ilkorin/murilind). See the entry on i-affection for further discussion.
A Doriathrin noun meaning field, valley (Ety/NAD), also appearing as nan and described as land at foot of hill with many streams (EtyAC/NAD).
An Ilkorin place name appearing in The Etymologies from the 1930s, likely a combination of valley and the name (Ety/DAY).
A Doriathrin noun for web (Ety/NAT). Its Quenya cognate MQ. indicates a primitive form *natse, where the [ts] became [ss] because medial voiceless stops became [s] before [s] in Ilkorin.

A Doriathrin word for Dwarf derived from the root MNAUK- or (Ety/NAUK). Tolkien said that it was a diminutive form, not a direct cognate of MQ. or N. . It may be derived from a primitive form such as *naukle, as suggested by Helge Fauskanger (AL-Doriathrin/naugol), though there isnt enough evidence to determine the original final vowel, since primitive final vowels vanished in Ilkorin. The final -ol appeared because [o] developed between a consonant and final [l] in Ilkorin.

Its form naugla appears as an element in Dor. Necklace of the Dwarves (Ety/NAUK).

A Doriathrin noun meaning face derived from the root M (Ety/NIB). The vowel change suggests a primitive form *niba, where the [i] became [e] because of Ilkorin a-affection. If this is the case, it is not a direct cognate of N. front, face.

The Doriathrin number three attested only as an element in the word beech = three trunks (Ety/NEL). Its cognates MQ. and N. indicates a primitive form *nelede, which would have become Ilk. neld due to the Ilkorin syncope, as suggested by Helge Fauskanger (AL-Doriathrin/neldor).

A Doriathrin adjective for wise, magical derived from the root M (Ety/NGOL, THIN). In an earlier version of this entry, the forms were ngul and gul, but these were rejected (EtyAC/NGOL). It may be that Tolkien was considering making this another case where long [o] became [u] in Ilkorin, but he rejected the idea. In the entry for NGOL in The Etymologies, it appeared as both ngol and gol; the first of seems to be a variant of the usual rule that initial [g] became [g] in Ilkorin.

englishWord: one of the wise folk, Gnome
descriptionText: A Doriathrin name for the MQ. from the same primitive root MNGOLOD (Ety/NGOLOD). In the entry for NGOLOD in The Etymologies, it appeared as (n)gold, indicating a variation of the usual rule that initial [g] became [g] in Ilkorin. The second [o] of the primitive form was lost due to the Ilkorin syncope. Its genitive form golda also appeared as an element in the name *Noldo-jewel = Silmaril.

englishWord: one of the wise folk, Gnome

descriptionText: A Doriathrin noun for magic, lore from the primitive root M (Ety/NGOL), most likely from the primitive form *golwe based on its Quenya cognate MQ. . In the entry for NGOL in The Etymologies, it appeared as (n)golo, indicating a variation of the usual rule that initial [g] became [g] in Ilkorin. After its final vowel was lost, the final [w] became [u], which then became [o], the only Doriathrin example of this second change.

A Doriathrin noun for horror derived from the root MNGOROTH (Ety/NGOROTH). Its Noldorin cognate N. indicates a primitive form *gorotho, where the second o was lost due to the Ilkorin syncope. Ordinarily, an initial ng- became g- in Ilkorin, as noted by Helge Fauskanger (AL-Doriathrin/ngorth), and ngorth seems to be a variation on this rule.
A Doriathrin adjective meaning horrible, a combination of horror with the adjective suffix -in (Ety/NGOROTH).

A Doriathrin word meaning forward or west, derived from the root M (Ety/NIB). It could have developed from primitive forms like *nibon or *nibn(), with -on developing in the second example because [o] developed between a consonant and a final [n] in Ilkorin. As noted by Helge Fauskanger (AL-Doriathrin/nivon), the sense west probably developed from the meaning forward because the Elves thought of themselves as facing West when marking directions.
A Doriathrin noun for nose derived from M (Ety/LIW). It is likely an example of how , especially if the [e] first became [i] before the [g], as suggested by Helge Fauskanger (AL-Doriathrin/niw).
Of the few grammatical inflections for Ilkorin attested in The Etymologies, almost all of them have to do with nouns.

An adjective meaning hideous, horrible derived from the root M (Ety/ULUG). Its Telerin cognate MT. indicates a primitive form *ulga, so that in the Ilkorin word the short [u] became [o] preceding the final [a] before that final vowel vanished.
Apparently a masculine suffix attested in the name .

A noun for blood derived from the root M (Ety/YAR). Its cognates MQ. and N. indicates a primitive form *yar() [jar], where the vowel changed to [o] because of Ilkorin a-affection. Helge Fauskanger suggested instead that the primitive form was *yara because of the Quenya stem form yar-, with a lengthening of the vowel in the primitive monosyllabic form (AL-Ilkorin/or) @@@ examine further.

A Doriathrin noun for tree derived from the root MOR-NI or MORON (Ety/OR-NI, EtyAC/NEL). According Tolkien, it was in Doriath used especially of beech, but as a suffix [it was] used of any tree of any size (Ety/OR-NI). The root MOR-NI in The Etymologies suggests a primitive form of Morni, but elsewhere Tolkien indicated the primitive form was Morne (e.g. on SD/302). Both primitive forms would have produced Ilk. orn, as noted by Helge Fauskanger (AL-Doriathrin/orn).

A Doriathrin noun for mountain derived from the root MOROT (Ety/OROT). Its Old Noldorin cognate ON. suggests a primitive form *oroto, where the second [o] was lost due to the Ilkorin syncope [orto]. Later the [t] became [] (th) because in Ilkorin. Both these developments were noted by Helge Fauskanger (AL-Doriathrin/orth). This word has two distinct plural forms attested: Dor. orthin (Ety/OROT) and Ilk. urthin (EtyAC/WATH); this could represent distinct rules for the formation of in the two dialects.

Apparently an abstract noun suffix appearing in the words and , perhaps of the same origin as the abstract endings MQ. and N. , though Helge Fauskanger suggested instead that it is related to the locative suffix MQ. (AL-Ilkorin/thalos).
A noun for war derived from primitive M (Ety/OKTA). It is a good example of how in Ilkorin, in this case [kt] > [x] (or []) > [].

There are quite a few attested plurals in The Etymologies for both Doriathrin and Ilkorin nouns. From these we can deduce a number of features for the Ilkorin and Doriathrin plurals.

The plural suffix : With two exceptions (see below), all the attested plurals in both Doriathrin and Ilkorin use the suffix -in. This seems to be the basic mechanism of plural formation for nouns. It is likely this suffix was inspired by the Gnomish plural suffix .

The i-affection of [a] and [o]: The plurals of Ilkorin nouns containing short vowels [a] and [o] have these vowels shift to [e] and [u] according to the normal rules of Ilkorin i-affection. The clearest examples of this change are Ilk. pl. lelmin (Ety/ALAM) and Ilk. pl. thurnin (Ety/THOR). This change did not occur for long vowels, such as Ilk. pl. torin (Ety/BAL); long [a] did not normally occur in Ilkorin.

This i-affection does not seem to occur for plurals in the Doriathrin dialect: Dor. roth pl. rodhin (Ety/ROD) and Dor. than gen. pl. thanion (LR/405). In fact, there is one noun that has plurals in both Ilkorin and Doriathrin, with Ilk. pl. urthin (EtyAC/WATH) versus Dor. pl. orthin (Ety/OROT). This lack of i-affection seems only to be true of the noun plural and not the general phonological history of Doriathrin: consider Dor. and Dor. , in which an older [a] became [e] before an [i].

Syncope of vowels in final syllables: In polysyllabic Ilkorin nouns, the vowel in the final syllable is lost when the plural suffix is added: Ilk. pl. edrin (Ety/ATA) and Ilk. pl. telmin (Ety/TAL). The i-affection of [a] and [o] noted above also applied in these cases. This change did not occur when the result would be an invalid cluster of vowels: Ilk. pl. Balthorin (Ety/BAL), but could occur where the cluster was acceptable: Ilk. pl. genglin (Ety/NGAN).

Note that there are no attested examples of plurals for polysyllabic Doriathrin nouns, so it is unclear whether this rule would apply to that dialect. However, based on the syncope in the genitive inflection Dor. naugla (Ety/NAUK), it seems likely that this rule would apply to Doriathrin as well.

Preservation of stem forms: In some nouns, older stem forms were preserved in the plural. For example, in Doriathrin a , such as Mroda > [ro >] Dor. roth (Ety/ROD, EtyAC/ROD). The older form [ro] is preserved in its plural form rodhin. Similarly, the word Dor. holly-tree still uses its simpler form holly in its plurals: Dor. pl. regin and gen. pl. region (Ety/EREK).

Plural using only i-affection: There is one Ilkorin plural produced exclusively by i-affection without the suffix -in: Ilk. pl. tel (Ety/TAL). Without further examples, however, it is unclear when this variant plural would or would not occur.

A Doriathrin word for east, derived from the root M back, return (Ety/RAD). It could have developed from primitive forms like *radon or *radn(), with -on developing in the second example because [o] developed between a consonant and a final [n] in Ilkorin. As noted by Helge Fauskanger (AL-Doriathrin/radhon), the sense east probably developed from the meaning back because the Elves thought of themselves as facing West when marking directions, so that East was behind them.
A Doriathrin place name appearing in The Etymologies from the 1930s, a combination of east and border (Ety/RAD, RI).

A word meaning flow, course of river derived from the root M (Ety/RAT). It probably developed from an nasal-infixed variant of the root such *ranta, as suggested by Helge Fauskanger (AL-Ilkorin/rant).

A Doriathrin noun for holly attested only in the plural forms regin and region (Ety/EREK). It also appeared as an element in the word holly-tree. It seems that the latter word replaced reg in the singular, and the original survived only in the plurals, as suggested by Helge Fauskanger (AL-Doriathrin/regorn).
A Doriathrin noun meaning holly-tree, a combination of (archaic?) holly and tree (Ety/EREK, OR-NI).
A Doriathrin variation of appearing in The Etymologies from the 1930s (Ety/EREK). It was translated Hollin and appears to be the genitive plural of Ilk. holly-tree.

A noun meaning a cut derived from the root M (Ety/RIS2). Its Quenya cognate MQ. suggests a primitive form *rista, where the [i] became [e] due to Ilkorin a-affection, as noted by Helge Fauskanger (AL-Ilkorin/rest).
A Doriathrin noun for precipice derived from primitive M (EtyAC/KHARAS), an example of how in Ilkorin.
A Doriathrin noun meaning edge, hem, border derived from the root MRI (Ety/RI). Its Quenya cognate MQ. suggests a primitive form *rima, where the primitive final vowel vanished in Ilkorin.

A Doriathrin noun meaning cold pool or lake (in mountains) derived from the root M (Ety/RINGI). Its Quenya cognate MQ. suggests a primitive form *ringwi [rigwi]. This is problematic, since , as with Dor. < Mlin(g)wi. It is possible, though, that this word developed directly from the root form *ringi [rigi], as suggested by Helge Fauskanger (AL-Doriathrin/ring).
A noun meaning domed roof derived from a nasal-infixed form of the root M roof, cave (Ety/ROD).
A Doriathrin noun meaning plain, wide land between mountains derived from the root M (Ety/ROS2).

A Doriathrin noun for cave, also appearing as roth, derived from primitive M or Mroda (Ety/ROD, EtyAC/ROD). The [d] spirantilized to [] (dh) as usual, then after the final vowel was lost the as suggested by Helge Fauskanger (AL-Doriathrin/roth). The original sound [] is preserved in the plural rodhin.
A noun for grass derived from the root M (Ety/SALAK). It is a good example of how in Ilkorin.

A noun meaning drinking-vessel derived from primitive M (Ety/SUK). This word went through a number of phonetic changes:

  • the [k] became [g] before the nasal [m]
  • the [u] shifted to [o] before the final [a]
  • the [g] vocalized to [u] before the nasal [m] producing the diphthong [ou]
  • the resulting diphthong [ou] became [au]

Helge Fauskanger originally suggested these developments (AL-Ilkorin/saum).
